titleStmt.title: The perplexing SB VIII 9683: solutions to textual uncertainties and a modern-era survival of a monobolon anchor in Egyptian Arabic?

div.head: Introduction
div.p:
In this paper, I address the textual problems surrounding P.Bodl.Ms.Gr.Class.c.42(P), a letter from Timotheos to Heron the centurion published by Henrik Zilliacus.
Zilliacus (1954). The letter addresses the attack of a certain Paulus together with a band of soldiers on a boat belonging to a monastery for an alleged unpaid debt. The soldiers removed the boat’s anchor along with two hundred jars of wine of its cargo. It is written in a profoundly unpolished Greek, which has posed difficulties to scholars. The problematic grammar and syntax contain elements that also appear in Coptic texts,
Cook (2015). pointing to an Egyptian-speaking milieu: consecutive uses of γάρ, καίπερ, misuse of cases, verb morphology and tenses, etc. The numerous repetitions and errors may also indicate the sender’s emotional distress and haste in response to the violent acts committed by soldiers.

The dealings with military officials (κεντυρίων, τριβοῦνος) and the soldiers mentioned may suggest either the existence of a local statio, the head of which was Heron the centurion, or the proximity to a military camp. The possible Memphite origin of the papyrus and the suggested approximate date (late 4th cent.) might hint at a detachment of the Legio V Macedonica stationed in Memphis from 293 until at least 399.
Zuckerman (1988).

To begin with, in line 2 of the ἐπιγραφή, as Leiv Amundsen had already suggested in the Apparatus to Zilliacus’ edition, Heron, the addressee of the letter, is most likely a centurion. Zilliacus credits Amundsen with the restoration κ̣εντυ̣ρ̣[ί]ο̣ν̣[ι. The proposal is supported by Malcolm Choat,
Choat (2000: 159 with n. 25). who correctly notes that the incident described involves soldiers, with a tribune mentioned in the final greetings.
For the replacement of the older φυλακῖται, the creation of the stationes, and the involvement of the Roman army in local affairs, as well as the role of centurions, see Bagnall (1977). For an in-depth approach to the role of the military in Roman Egypt, see Alston (1998).

Although the intention of the addresser is clear, the ink traces are hard to reconcile with a complete κεντυρίονι or κεντυρίωνι, due to a diagonal (almost horizontal) stroke, a part of which can be seen under the tau of κεντ. I would suggest that this is a stroke marking the abbreviated form of χ(αίρειν), and therefore, the word κ̣εντ([υρίωνι)] could have been abbreviated at the tau.
The abbreviation of χαίρειν in the 4th and 5th centuries takes various forms, with the most common being the following: Figure 1.

The above indicative comparison allows us to visualize the type of χαίρειν in the text. The traces appear to fit the BGU III 899 type with an almost horizontal stroke, running low through the chi. Figure 2.

Probably, there was an additional element, represented by the detached, almost vertical stroke, perhaps from a slimmer S-type abbreviation. At any rate, the restoration of χ̣(α̣ί̣ρ̣ε̣ι̣ν̣) appears justified.
I now turn to a commentary of the difficult parts of the text that require explanation.

div.head: Commentary
div.p: 4. Παῦλος τῶν στρατιωτῶν. I propose reading <μετὰ> τῶν στρατιωτῶν as Paulus could not have acted by himself given the volume of the items taken away. Line 18 indicates that there were more of them, despite the doubtful grammar. Although the name is too common to draw any inferences, a certain Flavius Paulus, soldier of the vexillatio of the legio V Macedonica stationed in Memphis, is known from a “contemporary” document (381 CE), W.Chr. 380 = P.Gen. I2 70, leasing abandoned land in Philadelphia. These small pieces of evidence enhance the Memphis connections, and it is therefore possible that we are seeing the same man in action.

4–5. μονόβολον: This term for a type of light single-fluked grapnel is very likely to have survived in the form of the Egyptian Arabic manabel (plural of mambal) known from the beginning of the twentieth century. It was apparently made from iron or wood and could be fixed into the shore by a swimmer, for which, see Basch (1985: 457–58). Corroborating evidence for its appearance is provided in line 9 of P.Lond. III 1164 (212 CE), a misthoprasia of a ship, listing its equipment, ἀνκύραις (l. ἀγκύραις) σιδηραῖς δυσὶ σὺν σπάθαις σιδηραῖς κ(αὶ) μονοβό̣λ̣ῳ ἑνὶ (‘together with two iron anchors with iron flukes and a monobolon’), where the single-fluked anchor follows the double-fluked one. For this information, Basch draws from Colin (1922: 72 with n. 2). Colin rejects the etymology proposed by R. Dozy, Supplément aux Dictionnaires Arabes, s.v. Picture 17, from the late-Latin venabulum via Spanish venable, and prefers to ascribe its origin to Arabic through the term for the arrow Picture 18.
Figure 3.

It is possible that the corruption of Greek μονόβολον into Egyptian Arabic manbal (=mambal) is due to a false etymology, consisting of the prefix mu- (for the participle) + نَبَلَ [nabala], ‘to shoot arrows.’ Perhaps, the act of throwing the single-fluked anchor to affix it to the shore was associated with shooting as a semantically similar action together with their phonetic proximity, hence the misconception. For numerous cases of folk etymologies with emphasis on Greek, see Fliatouras (2017), and Filos (2019).
The word is also attested in the Coptic Miracles of Saint Menas, for which see Piwowarczyk (2021: 534 n. 3), with a further discussion of the hitherto known sources on this lemma.

5-6. The edition has τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἡμῶν. Ἄπα Ὧρος τον | διακωνοις (l. τῶν διακόνων) τ̣οῖς Ἀνγυρωνιτης (l. τῆς Ἀγκυρωνίτου). The use of cases in the text is almost random. I propose a change in punctuation and a different interpretation, which better regularizes the syntax and improves the content: τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν Ἄπα Ὧρον τὸν διάκονον τῶν Ἀγκυρωνιτῶν.
διακώνοις → διάκωνος (l. διάκονος). What the editor took for an iota is the vertical left element of the bipartite sigma.
τ̣οῖς Ἀνγυρωνίτης = τοῖς Ἀγκυρωνίταις l. τῶν Ἀγκυρωνιτῶν contrary to Amundsen’s ‘τῆς Ἀγκυρωνίτου v. -ίτιδος sc., μονῆς.’ Phonetically, an interchange between η and αι is possible as an [e] sound.

ὑπὲρ → ἅ̣περ vel ὅ̣περ (l. καίπερ). The upsilons here do not have such hooks or loops at their base. It appears to be an erroneously formed concessive conjunction καίπερ since it introduces an adversative clause. Although typically καίπερ requires a participle, in the Roman period and thereafter, constructions with verbs are not that rare in the papyri, e.g., P.Brem. 48.4–6 (118 CE): καίπερ πολλ[ὰ] ἐκ[ι]ν|δύνευσα ἀπὸ χειμῶνος σφοδροῦ | κατὰ τοῦ βί[ο]υ; P.Ant. II 87.18 (late 3rd cent.): καί]περ μέχρι νῦν οὐ παρέσ̣τ̣η̣σαν; P.IFAO. II 27.5 (end of 5th–beginning of 6th cent.): κ]αίπερ ἤκουσα ὅτι μέλλει Εὐπράξιος; SB XXVIII 17239.9 (circa 567): μεθʼ ὃ καίπερ ἐκεῖνοι τὸν ἀΐδιον ἐπιγινώσκειν Θεὸν ὑπεστρέφοντο τῶν ἐξουδενώσεως εἰδώ[λων.
The clause is also attested in the Edict of Alexander Severus, SB XIV 11648 = P.Fay. 20.42, where the current text re-edited by Oliver (1978) has καίπερ κεκμηκ<ότ>α restoring a participle (explained in p. 481), unnecessarily in my opinion, as the reading in Schubart (1941: 45–49), καίπερ κέκμηκα with a verb, is (in theory) acceptable in this period. The Greek conjunction καίπερ is known to have been employed in Coptic with all kinds of verb forms and clauses,
Müller (2009: 142–144). and therefore, we might be seeing here a bilingual interference in terms of syntax.

9. ἀτενίστον (l. ἀτενίστων): This enigmatic term puzzled the editor, who did not adopt Amundsen’s proposal of a corrupted ἀγενίστων for ἀγεμίστων. There are three ways of interpreting it, starting with the most likely:

(a) ἀγενιστον (l. ἀναγνωστῶν): the most phonetically complex hypothesis but not entirely unlikely due to the language of the text. The ἀναγνῶσται are lower in rank than διάκονοι, and therefore, this would fit the sequence: πρεσβύτεροι, διάκονοι, ἀναγνῶσται. However, although the text is incomprehensible at moments, it does not contain such severe irregularities and corrupt forms.

(b) ἀγένιστοι (l. ἀγένειαστοι), meaning ‘beardless’ and, therefore, ‘an adolescent.’ There is the common adjective ἀγένειος, but there is also the verb γενειάζω. A vernacular formation is not entirely impossible, given the fact that the adjective ἀγένιαστος exists in some Modern Greek idioms, such as that of Corfu and Paxoi. Child and adolescent monks have been the subject of considerable controversy, and their presence was generally not welcome. But each community could set its own rules.
Talbot (2018).

(c) ἀτενιστον (l. ἀτενιστῶν) < ἀτενισταί: contrary to Zilliacus’ ἀτένιστοι. Deverbal nouns derived from -ίζω verbs usually end in -ιστής or -ιστήρ. Zilliacus wondered whether this term denotes a category of monks. This is a possibility as ἀτενίζειν has been employed in both Christian and Pagan religious texts, meaning ‘having an insight/gazing into the divine.’
A plethora of attestations and examples of various usages can be found in Strelan (1999). The selected examples are taken from his paper. For example, consider a Hermetic use:
Corpus Hermeticum 13.3 (Nock). καὶ πάντων ὅσα δὲ κατανοεῖς ἀτενίζων σωματικῇ ὁράσει (‘of everything that you perceive gazing with bodily eyesight’). In the neo-Platonic sphere, it is also used by Plotinus in the context of a soul’s contemplation of the divine:
Plot. Enn. 4.7.10. (Henry & Schwyzer). χαίρετ’, ἐγὼ δ’ ὑμῖν θεὸς ἄμβροτος πρὸς τὸ θεῖον ἀναβὰς καὶ τὴν πρὸς αὐτὸ ὁμοιότητα ἀτενίσας (‘Greetings, I am an immortal god for you, having ascended to the divine and gazed upon its similarity to me’). Themistius provides another indication of who these ἀτενισταί may have been, which almost amounts to a definition: οἱ σφόδρα ἐπιθυμοῦντες ἀτενίσαι πρὸς τὸν θεόν.
Them. Or. 4. (Schenkl). The same notion of the soul’s connection with the divine is found in Gregory Nyssenus: πρὸς τὸ θεῖον εἶχε τὴν ψυχὴν ἀτενίζουσαν.
Greg. Nyss. Contra Eunomium 3.9.13 (Jaeger).
10. αὐτοῦ → αὐτός (l. αὐτοῖς), cf. the identical bipartite sigma in line 9 in πρεσβυτέροις. Figure 4.

11. ἐπροσφώνησεν: the meaning of προσφωνέω in this text appears to be “promise”, with a very close parallel of such use being found in P.Köln II 109.15–16
See 15n., where the various meanings of the verb are discussed. (Christian letter, late 4th-early 5th cent. AD), in a similar linguistically problematic context. For the false augment in compounds, see a brief note in Mandilaras, (1973: 252).

11-12. Ἄπα Αἰ̣|αντῖνος → Ἄπα ⟦Ἀν̣⟧Ἀντίνος (l. Ἀντίνοος). The possibility of a scribal error involving the name Ἀντίνος, which commenced the following line, was noted by J. Gascou and R. Pintaudi in P.Bingen 121, n. 12.
For further bibliography on the papyrological finds in North Saqqara cf. n. 4. Looking closer at the digital image, we may reasonably conclude that the author attempted to delete an initial αν as he thought it would be better if the name was written in full in the next line. It is, therefore, quite possible that Apa Antinos is the known founder of the Memphite monastery. The few surviving documents, which constitute a small archive [TM Arch id: 457], were published by J. Gascou and R. Pintaudi in the aforementioned P.Bingen 121–126, with the earliest, P.Bingen 121, dated to the end of the fourth–beginning of the fifth century. P.Bingen 121, a letter addressed to Apa Antinos himself, also deals with individuals belonging to the Roman army (praepositus, princeps, στρατιώτης, κάστρον) as in our text too. However, the identification is not entirely secure. In our text the reference to Apa Antinos may be interpreted in two ways: (a) he is the superior of the monastery of Ancyronitans; (b) Horigenes said that Apa Antinos promised to give the sum to the superior of Ancyronitans. Interpreting this information is as difficult as interpreting the text itself.

16–17. δια|λήσασθαι (l. διαλύσασθαι) or perhaps δια<λα>λήσασθαι. It is possible that the prepositional phrase μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ hints at this meaning (lit. ‘discuss with him’). A sort of haplography could have occurred, hence the form διαλήσασθαι. However, the intention of a “solution” to the problems that have arisen is perfectly compatible with the text.
17–18. ἐπὶ γὰρ Κόμον ἢ τὸν πλοῖον αὐτοῦ | οἴνου. This passage requires reconsideration:
ἐπὶ → ἐπὶ (l. ἐπεὶ), which fits the narrative better.

Κόμον → κόμον (l. γόμον), ‘cargo’. It is reasonable to interpret the word as a reference to the ship’s cargo of wine jars (γόμος) and not a name, cf. P.Mich. XX 813.6 (373) μετ’ ἐγγύου τῆς τοῦ κόμου (l. γόμου) παραδώσεως. For the interchange of voiceless and voiced velar stops, see Gignac, Grammar I, 77–80.
ἢ → ἦ (l. ἦν): it appears this is the 3rd person singular Imperfect tense of εἰμὶ with the subject being the πλοῖον. For the omission of the final ν, see Mandilaras (1973: 111).

18. οἱ στρατιωτη for οἱ στρατιῶται: another example supporting the interchange between η and αι. Reading it as a plural form rather than a singular ὁ στρατιώτης is more plausible considering the facts, despite the singular ἀφήρπαξεν in the following line. It seems that in the author’s mind Paulus was the head of a band of soldiers, hence the mistaken singular form here. This agrees with line 4 Π̣α̣ῦλος τον στ[ρ]ατιωτο̣̣͂ν (l. μετὰ τῶν στρατιωτῶν) ἀφήρπαξεν, where again a singular form is used.
20. ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν Ὀνουων ἐστὶ ἁλιεὺς ἡμῶν → ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν Ὀνουῶν (l. Ὀνῶν). ἐσσ̣ι (l. ἐστι) ἁλιεὺς ἡμῶν. For attestations of the Egyptian name Ὀνῶς, see TM Nam 559.

Ἐσσί for ἐστί is not merely a phonetic error but a true variant as it occurs in a number of texts in the Roman period: BGU II 285.5–6 (2nd–3rd cent. CE) ἐν νόῳ ἔχῃς ὅτι ἡ θυγά[τ]ηρ μου ἰς (l. εἰς) Ἀλεξάνδρειαν | ἐσσί; BGU II 602.8 (2nd cent. CE) μάθε ἠ (l. εἰ) καθαρόν ἐσσι; P.Harr. II 235.10–11 (3rd–4th cent. CE) ἐ̣ν̣ τῷ Ὀξυρυ̣γ̣χείτῃ̣ ἐ̣σσὶν … γράφω Σαιράμμωνει (l. Σεράμμωνι) ὅπου ἐσσὶν παιρὶ (l. περὶ) τούτου; SB V 8027.10 (2nd–3rd cent. CE) ὁ σκυλμὸς γὰρ οὐκ ἔσσι \μι/κρές (l. μικρός); SB XII 10801.4–5 (3rd cent. CE) πρὸς τούτοις ἐσσὶ ἀσφα|λίσαι ἀραβῶνα (l. ἀρραβῶνα). It also appears in a quasi-literary ostracon from Xeron Pelagos in the Eastern desert O.Xer. inv. 48.6–7 (2nd cent. CE) σκώπτιν (l. σκώπτειν) οὐκ ἐσ|σιν. Mandilaras (1973: 106 n.1) mentions the equivalence of ἐσσί = ἐστίν only in a footnote with reference to Crönert (1903: 253), who records the said two BGU examples without elaborating further. It is a phenomenon perhaps worth exploring further.

22. ε̣ἴ̣σ̣ε̣ται διὰ αὐτοῦ → ε̣ἰ̣ς̣ τὰ ἴδια αὐτοῦ, that is ‘his hometown/community’ or, more generally, his ‘legal domicile.’ On the concept of ἴδια, see Braunert (1955/6). A few examples: SB X 10240.3–4: ἡ μήτηρ σου παρακαλ[ε]ῖ σε | ἐλθεῖν [εἰ]ς τὰ ἴδια; P.Apoll. 26.12: καὶ ἀναχωρήσῃ ἕκαστος εἰς τὰ ἴδια; SB XVIII 13867 col. II.48–49: ἀναβῆναι παρʼ ἐ|μὲ ὡς εἰς τ̣ὰ ἴδια; SB XX 15091.9–10: ἐθαύμασα δὲ τὴν σὴν καλοκἀγαθίαν ἕως τῆς δεῦρο μὴ ἐπανελθεῖν | εἰς τὰ ἴδια.
26. τριβοῦνον → τριβουνων (l. τριβοῦνον)

27. των Κω̣φίω → τω νυμ̣φίω (l. τὸν νυμφίον). In the context of greetings sent to a family, I would exclude a relatively rare name Νύμφιος (unattested in Egypt),
Apparently, the name of Oscan origin, a Hellenized form of Nium(p)sis, used to be popular in Greco-Roman Naples, for which, see Leiwo (1995: 76). and would understand it as ‘son-in-law’ or ‘bridegroom’, the former being more likely, unless a wedding is hinted at.

32v. πραὰ → No transcribable traces of a παρὰ are left on the papyrus, apart, perhaps, from a possible abbreviation stroke, hence π̣(αρὰ). The origin of this reading must be a confusion of the name Ἥρων written in line 2 under the end of line 1, which indeed could have been mistaken for a πραα: Figure 5.
Therefore, it should be removed from the transcription.

p.seg: A tentative regularized version of the text

div.p: Τῷ δεσπότῃ μου καὶ ὡς ἀληθῶς τιμίῳ πάτρωνι ἀδελφῷ Ἥρωνι κεντυρίωνι, χαίρειν. Τιμόθεος. Παῦλος μετὰ τῶν στρατιωτῶν ἀφήρπαξεν τὸ μόνοβολον τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ ἡμῶν Ἄπα Ὧρου, τοῦ διακόνου τῶν Ἀγκυρωνιτῶν, καίπερ οὐδὲν χρεωστεῖ αὐτῷ, εἰ μὴ μόνον δισχιλίας τετρακοσίας μυριάδας. Καὶ πολλοῖς μονάζουσιν, ἀναχωρηταῖς καὶ πρεσβυτέροις και διακόνοις και ἀναγνωστῶν ἀριθμίῳ, καὶ αὐτοῖς γὰρ διαφέρει τὸ μονόβολον. Καὶ εἶπεν Ὡριγένης ὅτι προσεφώνησεν ἄπα Ἀντίνῳ/ἄπα Ἀντίνος τῷ πρεσβυτέρῳ μονῆς Ἀγκυρωνιτῶν τὰς δισχιλίας τετρακοσίας μυριάδας. Καὶ ὁ προκουράτωρ αὐτοῦ οὐδὲν ἔλαβεν, εἰ μὴ μόνον χιλίας διακοσίας μυριάδας. Ἀξιῶ καὶ παρακαλῶ σε, δέσποτα, ποίησον αὐτὸν ἐκεῖνον τὸν Παῦλον ἐλθεῖν εἰς Θελβὼ καὶ διαλύσασθαι μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ, ἐπεὶ γόμος ἦν τοῦ πλοῖου αὐτοῦ οἶνος. Καὶ οἱ στρατιῶται τὸν ὁδεύοντα οὐ μόνον, <ἀλλὰ καὶ> διακόσια διπλᾶ μεγάλα ἀφήρπαξαν. Καὶ ἐφ᾽ ὃ κέλευσον τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν Ὀνῶν. Ἔστιν ἁλιεύς ἡμῶν. Ἀξιῶ οὖν, δέσποτα, κέλευσον αὐτὸν ἐλθεῖν εἰς τὰ ἴδια αὐτοῦ. Ἐὰν θελήσῃς πάλιν ἐλθεῖν ἐπὶ τὸ κρίμα, ἐλθὲ ὅπου θέλῃς. Καὶ γὰρ σὺ <ἦς> ὁ πάτρων τοῦ πλοίου αὐτοῦ, ὅτε κατεῖχεν αὐτὸ ἐν Ἡρακλέους. Σὺ γὰρ διαλυθῆναι αὐτῷ αὔξεις. Πολλὰ προσαγορεύω, δέσποτα ἄδελφε, προσαγορεύω τὸν κύριον τὸν τριβοῦνον καὶ τὸν νυμφίον καὶ πάντας ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ ὑμῶν.
Ἐρρῶσθαί σε εὔχομαι πολλοῖς χρόνοις. Διευτύχει.
V: Τῷ δεσπότῃ μου καὶ ὡς ἀληθῶς τιμίῳ πάτρωνι ἀδελφῷ Ἥρωνι
Π(αρὰ) Τιμοθέου.
To my master and truly esteemed patron and brother Heron the centurion, greetings (from) Timotheos.

Paulus, together with the soldiers, took away the monobolon of our brother Apa Horos, deacon of the Ancyronitans, although he owes him nothing but two thousand four hundred myriads. And it is important to many monks, anchorites, presbyters, deacons and the numerous lectors, since the monobolon also belongs to them. Horigenes said that he promised to give Apa Antinos, the presbyter of the monastery of Ancyronitans, the two thousand four hundred myriads; and his procurator had received nothing but one thousand two hundred myriads. I request and implore you, master, have Paulus come to Thelbo and resolve it with him since the ship’s cargo was wine. And the soldiers did not only do this to the carrier, but also took away two hundred large dipla. In this matter, command our brother Onos, our fisherman, to come. I beg you, master, order him to go to his domicile. If you want to come again to give judgment, come wherever you want. Since you were the patron of this ship, when he seized it in Heracleopolis, you will exert greater power in resolving it with him. Many greetings, master and brother. I also greet the tribune and his son-in-law, and everyone in your family.
Verso: To my master and truly esteemed patron and brother Heron.
From Timotheos.
